title: What Is Recovery Like After Endoscopic Transsphenoidal Surgery?
metaDescription: Recovery after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery: hospital stay, a blocked nose, hormone checks, activity limits, and CSF leak signs. Ask your surgeon.
excerpt: Most people leave hospital a few days after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery. Expect a blocked nose, fatigue, and hormone checks, and know which symptoms need a same-day call.

content.text: Recovery after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery is usually shorter than recovery after a craniotomy, because the tumour is reached through the nose and there is no large scalp incision. Most people stay in hospital for about two to four days, go home with a blocked, crusty nose, and need two to six weeks before desk work feels normal. Heavy lifting, nose blowing, and flying wait until your surgeon clears them. Hormone checks matter as much as the nose: urine output, sodium, and cortisol are watched because endoscopic pituitary surgery sits next to the pituitary gland.

The ranges below are what many patients experience after removal of a pituitary adenoma. They are not a promise. Vision recovery after pituitary surgery follows its own timeline and is not the same as nasal healing. A cerebrospinal fluid repair, unstable sodium, or a larger tumour can stretch recovery. Your surgeon sets the exact limits for your case.
How Long Does Recovery Take After Endoscopic Transsphenoidal Surgery?

People searching for pituitary surgery recovery time usually want a week-by-week picture, not a single number. Energy, nasal breathing, and hormones recover on different clocks. Smell and stamina can still be improving at two or three months, even when the nasal wound has sealed.

items: Day 0 to 1: neurological checks, pain control, and measurement of how much you drink and pass urine. The nose feels blocked. Blood-stained mucus is common.
Days 2 to 4: many people go home once they are drinking, sodium is stable, pain is controlled, and there is no clear watery drip from the nose.
Weeks 1 to 2: congestion, crusts, fatigue, and a dull sense of taste. Walk, rest, and use saline only as instructed. Do not blow your nose.
Weeks 3 to 6: breathing through the nose often eases. Many people return to desk work. Straining, heavy lifting, and contact sport stay off until you are cleared.
6 to 12 weeks: smell, taste, and stamina may still be catching up. Hormone tablets are reviewed. An MRI is often planned around three months, on your surgeon's schedule.

content.text: What Is the Hospital Stay Like?

The hospital stay after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery is there to catch problems that are easier to treat early. Nurses check alertness, headache, vision, nasal bleeding, temperature, and fluid balance. Blood tests track sodium. If the surgery opened the diaphragm above the pituitary, the team also watches for clear fluid that could be cerebrospinal fluid.

Pain is often a sinus pressure or frontal headache rather than a severe wound pain. It is usually managed with ordinary pain relief. You are asked to sit up and walk early, which lowers the chance of blood clots. Some surgeons place soft nasal splints or packing; others use only dissolvable material. If splints are used, they are often removed at an early clinic visit, not left in for the whole recovery.

You can usually wash your hair once you are home, because there is no scalp incision to keep dry. The restriction is the nose: do not let shower water blast into the nostrils, and do not pick crusts. Ask for written instructions before discharge, including which steroid tablets to take and which number to call overnight.
Why Is the Nose Blocked, and When Can You Blow It?

Nasal congestion after pituitary surgery is the complaint people mention most. The corridor used for surgery is swollen. Dried blood, mucus, and dissolvable packing sit in the nostrils, so you mouth-breathe, snore, and lose much of your sense of smell. A blood-stained discharge for one to two weeks is common. A sudden rush of bright red blood is not.

Do not blow your nose until your surgeon says you may, often for two to four weeks, and sometimes longer if a leak was repaired. Blowing raises pressure on the sellar repair. Sneeze with your mouth open. Do not insert tissues, fingers, or cotton buds. Saline spray or a gentle rinse is useful once your team starts it; starting a forceful rinse on your own can disrupt the repair.

Crusts are cleaned at follow-up, sometimes by an ENT colleague. Taste and smell are often dull for weeks and can take a few months to return. Most people improve, but a lasting change in smell is possible and should be discussed at review rather than assumed to be permanent in the first fortnight.
Thirst, Urine, Sodium, and Cortisol After Surgery
The pituitary controls water balance and several hormones, so recovery is not only nasal. Three patterns cause most of the urgent calls after people go home.

items: Diabetes insipidus: large volumes of pale urine and sudden, intense thirst, often in the first few days. It is often temporary. Some people need a short course of desmopressin. Call if you cannot keep up with the thirst, or if urine output becomes extreme overnight.

Low sodium: this can appear several days later, sometimes after discharge. Headache, nausea, and confusion are the usual clues. It is why sodium is rechecked even when you feel the nose is the only issue.

Low cortisol: surgery can temporarily reduce the signal that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol. Many people go home on hydrocortisone, with instructions to increase the dose if they vomit, have a fever, or need another procedure. Do not stop steroid tablets because you feel better.

content.text: Thyroid hormone, sex hormones, prolactin, and growth hormone are usually judged over the following weeks, not on the morning after surgery. If the operation was for acromegaly, prolactinoma, or Cushing disease, your endocrinologist times those blood tests to the disease, not to a generic calendar. Keep the same laboratory when you can, so results can be compared.
When Can You Work, Drive, Fly, or Exercise?

Desk work is often realistic at two to four weeks if fatigue, vision, and pain medicines allow it. Jobs with lifting, night shifts, or dusty air need longer. Driving waits until you are alert, your vision is safe for the road, and you are off sedating pain tablets. For many people that is around one to two weeks, but it is a decision for you and your surgeon, not a fixed date.

Flying after pituitary surgery is a common question for people treated in Dubai or Tehran and returning home. Cabin pressure and a blocked nose are uncomfortable, and a leak that is still open is a reason to delay. Many surgeons wait until a nasal check, often somewhere between two and six weeks, and longer if cerebrospinal fluid was seen at surgery. Do not book a non-changeable ticket until that clearance is in writing.

Walk from the first days at home. Avoid bending so your head is below your waist, heavy lifting, straining on the toilet, and contact sport until you are told the repair has healed, commonly four to six weeks. Constipation is worth preventing with fluids and the laxative your team suggests, because straining is the same pressure as lifting.
Warning Signs, Including a CSF Leak

A cerebrospinal fluid leak after transsphenoidal surgery is the symptom to take seriously the same day. Cerebrospinal fluid is clear and watery, not sticky mucus. It may drip more when you lean forward, and it can taste salty or metallic. A headache that is worse when you sit or stand and eases when you lie flat can go with it. Your surgeon may advise bed rest, a lumbar drain, or a repair. Do not wait for a routine clinic if this starts at home.

items: Clear watery drip from the nose, especially on leaning forward
A sudden increase in bright red nasal bleeding, or bleeding you cannot stop
Fever, neck stiffness, or a headache that is clearly worsening
New confusion, repeated vomiting, or a seizure
A drop in vision or new double vision. A sudden change needs a same-day call, even if sight had been improving
Extreme thirst with very large urine volumes, or headache with nausea in the week after discharge

Frequently Asked Questions
How long is the hospital stay after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery?

A straightforward stay is often two to four days. You go home when you are eating and drinking, walking, comfortable on simple pain relief, and your sodium and fluid balance are stable. A leak repair, hard-to-control thirst and urine output, or sodium that will not settle can add days. Leaving earlier is not a prize if those checks are unfinished, and staying longer does not mean the surgery failed.
How long will my nose stay blocked after pituitary surgery?

Expect mouth breathing for at least one to two weeks, and often longer. Swelling, crusts, and dissolving packing keep the airway narrow even after any splints are removed. Breathing usually improves through weeks three to six. Smell can lag behind airflow. A rinse or spray should follow your surgeon's timing. If one side blocks again after it had opened, or bleeding restarts, get that checked rather than clearing it yourself.
When can I blow my nose after transsphenoidal surgery?

Not in the first weeks, unless your own surgeon has given you an earlier date. Nose blowing, closed-mouth sneezing, and straining all raise pressure on the repair at the back of the nose. A common instruction is to wait two to four weeks, and longer after a leak repair. Until then, dab the nostrils, use the prescribed saline, and let crusts be cleaned in clinic. If you blow once by habit, call and describe what came out, especially if it was clear and watery.
What does a CSF leak feel like after this operation?

People often describe a sudden drip of clear fluid, like water, from one nostril when they sit up or lean forward. Mucus is thicker and does not usually flow in a steady watery stream. A salty or metallic taste and a headache that improves when you lie down are extra clues. Photograph nothing and do not pack the nose tightly. Sit up slightly if you have been told to, keep the fluid if you can catch a sample, and contact the surgical team the same day.
Why am I so thirsty and passing so much urine?

That pattern can be diabetes insipidus, a water-balance problem from temporary pituitary upset. Urine is pale and the volume is high, and thirst tracks it. It often settles over days. Some people need desmopressin for a short time, and a few need it for longer. Measure roughly how much you drink and pass, and call if you cannot match the losses or you become drowsy. A different problem, low sodium, can appear later with headache and nausea, so do not add extra salt or extra water on your own without a blood test.
When can I fly, drive, and go back to work?

Driving is often considered once you are alert, off strong pain tablets, and happy with your vision, commonly around one to two weeks. Desk work often fits at two to four weeks. Flying is the one to plan last: many people are asked to wait until a nasal review, frequently two to six weeks, and longer if there was a leak or you still have heavy congestion. Physical work, lifting, and sport follow the same clearance as straining, often four to six weeks. Ask for these three dates in writing before you leave hospital.
